newsitem.title: BERMUDA: RUGBY UNION - We'll be better this time - Puma prop.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION - We'll be better this time - Puma prop.

text.p: HAMILTON, June 27 - Roberto Grau, one of only three rugby professionals in the Argentinian team who end their tour of New Zealand on Saturday, believes the Pumas will be better equipped to handle the All Blacks "sevens style" game in the second test.

Front rower Grau, contracted for the rest of the year with Louis Luyt's Gauteng Lions (Transvaal), said a week's assessment of their 93-8 first-test loss had given his team-mates a clear indication of the requirements to compete with the All Blacks.
"It was unbelievable," he said of the All Blacks game at Athletic Park.
"We went there expecting a confrontation and they played sevens rugby and ran all around us enjoying themselves," the Pumas prop told NZPA.

"We've seen where we've gone wrong, we've seen where we've made the errors and we've talked about them quite a bit. We know what to do, but how well we do it will depend on how well we can keep our heads together.

"In Wellington we got hit by a high voltage and the shock just stunned us. We couldn't stop and think and say 'now let's pull together and do this or change that'. We played right into the hands of the All Blacks and we didn't change things when it
wasn't going right for us. That was very bad."

Grau, 26, relegated Springboks prop Balie Swart to the reserves bench in the Super 12 as soon as he recovered from a shoulder injury. He played in eight of their matches, and is now a senior statesman of the Pumas team.

At 1.82m and 105kg, Grau is not one of those usual burly or squat, thick-necked props with thighs like tree trunks. He's more a modern-day scrum anchorman who provides solidity in the forwards and performs the loose forwards' job around the field.
"I've always been the quicker type around the field and that's one reason why it didn't take me long to fit into Super 12 rugby.
"But I did find it (Super 12) different. I covered more yardage and I had to move quicker from point to point. I made more tackles and I played with ball in hand more."
Grau is well-versed in New Zealand rugby, having played against the Canterbury Crusaders and Waikato Chiefs and part of the matches against the Wellington Hurricanes and Auckland Blues.
But he said he was surprised with the speed and accuracy of the All Blacks game in the first test.

"They are very sharp. They're merciless when you make mistakes -- they just punish you to the maximum. That's the making of a great team. They move the ball with hell of a speed and skills. They're the best team in the world. They will beat the Springboks and the Wallabies -- no doubt."

Grau will be playing his 17th test at Hamilton's sold-out Rugby Park tomorrow night -- not bad for a kid who played as a goalkeeper in the soccer-mad South American country and earned the nickname of "Pato" -- after the legendary Ubeldo Fillol,
goalkeeper of the 1978 World Cup champion Argentinian team.
Grau hails from the same province, Cuyo, as the "raging bull from the pampas" Federico Mendez, who played for Natal before moving to big-spending English club Bath.
"I wanted to play professional rugby so I followed Mendez."
There could have been two Graus in the Pumas front row tomorrow.
Unfortunately, the other, Roberto's younger brother Martin, died in tragic circumstances a few years ago.
Martin Grau captained the Argentinian under-19 side in 1992 and was a reserve for the Pumas later that year.

But he died after a minor surgery to an elbow injury he received in rugby. The circumstances surrounding the surgery remains sketchy, but Roberto Grau decided after his brother's death that he would do well in the sport his brother loved.
